description: The window showing the server's own SPA. Its page is served by the subshell-server this app manages, so it is treated as REMOTE content: it may raise the assistant, drop its own title bar, show one notification, drag its window, open a page of THIS server in the system browser, read this app's own macOS permission states, read the app's own two update version facts — and, as the ONE deliberate exception to 'nothing that touches the service', switch who runs the server. That exception is argued in docs/security.md: a page already holding the admin restart route can do worse than move the server between two supervisors, and the assistant window that used to carry the act read as a bug. None of the others is a second exception. The browser one takes a PATH, refuses anything that could be a host, and joins it onto this window's own loopback origin, so it opens the server the page is already running in — something a person can do by typing the address. The permissions one (2026-09-14, the sixth) takes no argument at all and answers two questions about this app's own grants from the OS; it is here because two of the three moments a missing permission has to be explained are in this very page, and the written argument the count demands is spec 2026-09-14 section 7. The seventh (2026-09-17, spec 2026-09-17 section 5.3) is argued the same way and is even smaller: desktop_app_update takes no argument, runs no network, and answers currentVersion and availableVersion from this build's own package info and the one settings field the daily check already writes — it is here because the sidebar row that says 'an update is waiting' must know whether one is, and the app, not the server, is the only thing that knows its own version. It NEVER checks; asking the release source stays on the bundled page, and installing does too. Requesting a permission, opening a System Settings pane, and every update verb stay on the bundled page. Everything else that touches the CLI is absent by construction, not by convention.
